results.question: Compare the disk-induced tidal disruption-driven growth scenario for intermediate-mass black holes described in Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions (arXiv:2609.03701v2) with the stellar clustering / bound-companion analysis methods used in Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars (arXiv:2604.27382v2). Specifically: (1) What concrete dTDE mass supply rate and sensitivity to the disk outer radius does the Rapid Growth paper report? (2) What simulation/analysis capabilities from the Star cluster formation paper could be used to test or refine the assumptions about the stellar cusp and bound stellar populations feeding the IMBH in the Rapid Growth paper? Provide an explicit synthesis requiring supported facts from both papers.
results.reference_answer: (1) Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions reports that disk-induced stellar disruptions can sustain stellar disruption rates of ~ (1–3) × 10^−3 M☉ yr^−1, and that extending the disk outer radius from R_out = R_sg to R_out = 3 R_sg produces only a slight decrease in the dTDE-driven mass supply (from ~8×10^−4 to ~6×10^−4 M☉ yr^−1), i.e., the overall dTDE rate is only weakly dependent on R_out (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; 41d12c9455789b742b18e36e). (2) The Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars paper describes N-body models of gradual star cluster formation, post-processing to identify bound systems around massive stars, and constructing projected stellar density profiles to compare clustering predictions with observations (evidence: d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc; 3f5057c15ab6fdac9f804821). Synthesis: By combining these capabilities, one could supply the Rapid Growth model with more realistic initial conditions for the stellar cusp and local bound-companion population: the clustering paper’s N-body simulations and bound-companion identification methods can quantify the number, radial distribution, and projected density profiles of stars near massive objects at specified cluster ages, which would directly test the Rapid Growth assumption about the available stellar reservoir for disk capture and inward migration. This addresses a limitation noted in Rapid Growth that their simulations model the local dynamical feeding mechanism but require galaxy-scale inputs about the formation and lifetime of gas-rich nuclear environments (da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e). Together, the Star cluster formation methods could refine the Rapid Growth dTDE supply estimates by providing empirically motivated stellar spatial and dynamical distributions for use in the disk-capture and migration prescriptions (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc).
results.answer:
The Rapid Growth paper reports disk-induced tidal disruption (dTDE) stellar mass supply rates of order ≃ 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}. [1]

The Rapid Growth paper reports that the dTDE-driven stellar disruption rate is ≃ (1–3) × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1} (statement in the paper's conclusions). [2]

Wang et al. (Rapid Growth) give mass-dependent examples: for M• = 3 × 10^{3} M⊙ and 10^{4} M⊙ the disruption rates remain at ≃ 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}, while for M• = 3 × 10^{4} M⊙ the rate is ≃ 3 × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}. [3]

The Rapid Growth paper states that these dTDE mass-supply rates exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate for black holes with M• < 10^{5} M⊙. [2]

The Rapid Growth paper explicitly tested sensitivity to the inner accretion radius: comparing RdTDE = 10^{-4} pc (fiducial) with RdTDE = 5 × 10^{-5} pc produced nearly identical disruption rates, which the paper states indicates insensitivity to the specific choice of RdTDE (inner accretion radius). [4]

The Star Cluster Formation (TCCA) study uses high-precision N-body simulations of gradual star-cluster formation with an analytic gas potential (Turbulent Clump Core Accretion), controlled by parameters including star-formation efficiency per freefall time (ε_ff), clump mass M_cl and cloud mass surface density Σ_cloud, with gas mass linearly reduced to zero at the end of star formation t_★. [5] [6]

The Star Cluster Formation paper provides a routine to identify bound companions around a massive star by iteratively finding the closest bound companion, replacing the pair/triple with its center-of-mass, and continuing to build higher-order bound systems (binary → triple →...). [6]

The Star Cluster Formation work computes quantitative clustering metrics such as the mean number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ (with mass-threshold choices), reports uncertainties (16th–84th percentile spreads and standard errors), and presents these metrics at specified cluster ages (e.g., t = 3.0 Myr). [7] [8]

The Star Cluster Formation paper constructs projected stellar density profiles around massive stars to compare models with observations and to diagnose clustering around massive primaries. [9]

The Rapid Growth dTDE rates of ≃ (1–3) × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1} (52a69f9f) could be tested by supplying Wang et al.'s disk-capture and migration calculations with the star-cluster paper's quantitative inner-stellar-population outputs (e.g., ⟨N_bound⟩ and companion mass-thresholded distributions) to produce a matched estimate of the disk-crossing supply rate. [2] [7]

Wang et al. identify two-body relaxation refilling the disk-crossing population and formation of a stellar cusp as key processes controlling sustained dTDE rates; the Star Cluster Formation methods (the bound-companion identification and central/offset/ejected classification) can be used to quantify how many stars are bound and centrally concentrated and hence available to be scattered into disk-crossing orbits. [6] [10]

Because the TCCA models vary environmental parameters that set cluster compactness and velocity dispersion (Σ_cloud, M_cl, ε_ff), those N-body outputs can provide stellar distributions for different cluster compactnesses that could be combined with Wang et al.'s figure-level Rout variants (Rout = R_{sg} versus Rout = 3 R_{sg}) to probe how the dTDE supply rate responds to changes in disk outer radius across different stellar environments. [2] [6]

The Star Cluster Formation simulations produce time-resolved cluster snapshots (e.g., analyses at t = 3.0 Myr) while Wang et al. note their dTDE runs are limited in duration (~0.3 Myr) and that growth to ≳10^{5} M⊙ would require persistence of cluster and disk conditions for >30 Myr; therefore extending or using longer-duration N-body cluster models can directly test whether the dTDE rates reported by Wang et al. can be sustained on the >30 Myr timescale they identify as required for substantial IMBH growth. [4] [8]

The Rapid Growth paper's figure text includes disk-outer-radius variants labeled "Rout = Rsg" and "Rout = 3Rsg". [2]

retrieved_chunks.text:
## ABSTRACT 

Dense nuclear star clusters provide unique environments for studying the dynamical interactions between stars and massive black holes. When an accretion disk is present, dissipative star–disk interactions can capture surrounding stars, drive their inward migration, and ultimately lead to disk-induced tidal disruption events (dTDEs). The long-term feeding rate from this process, however, cannot be inferred from single-orbit migration estimates alone, as it depends on the coupled evolution of disk capture, collisional relaxation, stellar depletion and replenishment, and physical mergers within the star cluster. In this work, we use high-performance direct _N_ -body simulations combined with analytic prescriptions for star–disk interactions to follow this coupled evolution for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) with accretion disks embedded in dense stellar clusters. The simulations track the formation of the stellar cusp, the capture of stars by repeated disk crossings, their subsequent orbital damping and migration, and their eventual consumption by the central IMBH. We find that dTDEs can sustain stellar mass supply rates of _∼_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] , which exceeds the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate for IMBHs with _M• <_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . These results identify dTDEs as an efficient stellar feeding channel for IMBHs in gas-rich dense stellar systems. As one possible application, this mechanism may help transform _∼_ 10[3] _M⊙_ IMBHs into more massive black-hole seeds, provided that compact stellar clusters and accretion disks persist for _>_ 30 Myr.

retrieved_chunks.text: _Limitations and future work._ —Despite the insights provided by our simulations, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the conversion efficiency of disrupted stellar mass into black hole growth remains uncertain. Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of classical TDEs suggest accreted fractions of _∼_ 25%–43% for a 10[6] _M⊙_ SMBH disrupting stars of 1–300 _M⊙_ (Bu et al. 2023; Sheng et al. 2026). In our disk-induced TDE scenario, however, stars are delivered on nearly circular, coplanar orbits and migrate inward through the disk prior to disruption. This may lead to more efficient debris circularization and thus a potentially higher accreted fraction than that achieved in the highly eccentric, parabolic orbits typical of classical TDEs. Nevertheless, our current assumption of full accretion should be regarded as an optimistic upper limit. Second, the limited duration of our simulations raises the question of whether the seemingly steady dTDE rate measured over _∼_ 0.3 Myr can be sustained over 30 Myr required to grow an IMBH to _∼_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . This would require both a continuous external gas supply to maintain the disk and a sufficiently large stellar reservoir, from which stars can be continuously replenished into the diskcrossing region via two-body scattering among stars and dynamical friction against the ambient gas over long timescales ( _>_ 30 Myr). Third, our analytic treatment of star–disk interactions, while capturing the essential physics, omits important processes associated with embedded stars, such as gas accretion onto stars and stellar remnants, stellar winds, supernovae, and their feedback on the disk structure. These processes are not included

Wang et al. 

2 

disk interactions can act as a dissipative conveyor of stellar material: the disk captures stars from a threedimensional cluster, damps their orbits, and delivers them inward on a migration timescale. 

This mechanism is especially relevant for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). For _M•_ ≲ 10[5] _M⊙_ , the dTDE mass supply rate can exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate, and may therefore dominate the early mass budget of the black hole. The problem is not simply whether an individual star can be captured by the disk; that can be estimated from local drag and migration timescales. The central question is whether a realistic collisional stellar cluster can maintain a continuous supply of stars to the disk after the innermost stars have been consumed. The answer depends on several coupled processes: the formation of a stellar cusp around the IMBH, two-body relaxation that refills the disk-crossing population, stochastic few-body encounters, mass segregation and stellar evolution, and physical collisions among stars that captured by the disk. These effects determine both the dTDE rate and the mass spectrum of the disrupted stars.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS In this work, we investigate dTDEs as a stellar feeding channel for IMBHs embedded in gas-rich dense nuclear star clusters. By performing high-precision direct _N_ - body simulations with analytic prescriptions for star– disk interactions, we follow the coupled evolution of the stellar cusp, relaxation-driven replenishment, disk capture, inward migration, stellar mergers, and eventual accretion onto the central IMBH. We find that this process can sustain stellar disruption rates of _∼_ (1 _−_ 3) _×_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] , significantly exceeding the Eddington accretion rate for black holes with _M• <_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . The main conclusion is therefore that disk-induced stellar disruptions can provide an efficient and dynamically sustained stellar mass supply to IMBHs in compact gasrich stellar systems. _Choice of inner accretion radius._ —Due to computational limitations, we replace the tidal disruption radius _R_ t with a larger accretion radius _R_ dTDE. To assess the robustness of this treatment, we compare our fiducial model ( _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc) with a run adopting a smaller value, _R_ dTDE = 5 _×_ 10 _[−]_[5] pc (green curve), in Figure 8. The resulting disruption rates are nearly identical, indicating that our results are insensitive to the specific choice of _R_ dTDE. This insensitivity is physically expected: once stars are captured by the accretion disk, they settle onto nearly circular orbits and rapidly migrate inward. After crossing _R_ dTDE, they continue migrating toward the central IMBH and typically reach the tidal disruption radius _R_ t within _∼_ 10[4] yr. Therefore, as long as _R_ dTDE is sufficiently small, the resulting stellar disruption rate converges and is insensitive to the exact choice of _R_ dTDE.

Massive stars are formed randomly in the star cluster, i.e., approximating the process of Turbulent Core Accretion in the limit of no primordial mass segregation of massive star formation. We perform an analysis of clustering of companions around these massive stars. We also compare with observations and massive stars formed by Competitive Accretion in `STARFORGE` simulations. In addition, the simulations involve 50% of systems being primordial binaries, but with no preference for massive stars to be favored as being in multiples. There are no primordial triples or higher-order multiples, so such systems must form dynamically during the evolution of the cluster. We track the formation of such bound systems of companions around massive stars to study the effect of star cluster environment on the dynamical capture of companions. This exploration yields benchmark statistics that can be used to compare the results of more sophisticated MHD + _𝑁_ -body simulations to be developed in future studies.

## **5 CONCLUSIONS** 

Anosova J. P., 1986, Ap&SS, 124, 217 

- Appel S. M., et al., 2026, AJ, 172, 12 

In this paper, we studied the clustering of bound and unbound companions around massive stars inside gradually forming star clusters via “Turbulent Clump Core Accretion” (TCCA) by post-processing existing _𝑁_ −body simulations. In these simulations, star clusters are formed in different formation timescales ( _𝑡★_ ) parameterized by star formation efficiency per freefall time ( _𝜖_ ff), mass of star-forming clump ( _𝑀_ cl) and mass surface densities (Σcloud) of the parent cloud. 

We found that massive stars in the center of bound cluster gather more companions than massive stars that have been ejected from the cluster. We found that ejected stars are mostly single or in binaries. The number of companions is greater for massive stars in star clusters with lower stellar velocity dispersion and higher stellar densities. When we compared the clustering of companions around our massive stars with projected stellar density profiles, we found a good match to YSO profiles in the AFGL 5180 and G19.88-0.53 star-forming regions. Finally, we noted a lack of close triple companions around our simulated O-stars when compared to companions around O-stars in the `SMASH+` survey. Since these companions were not captured dynamically, they are likely formed via primordial routes like core or disk fragmentation. 

In the future, we aim to extend our gradual star cluster formation models with hydrodynamical coupling and an accurate treatment of primordial triples. We are also currently working on extending the analysis of dynamically gathered companions around primary stars across the full stellar mass spectrum.

## **2.2 Clustering around Massive Stars** 

We examine the stellar clustering around massive stars (≥ 8 _𝑀_ ⊙) formed in our simulations. To study the effect of cluster environment on such clustering, we divide these massive stars into three different subsets according to their location and boundedness. First, we determine stars that are bound to the star cluster using a snowballing algorithm developed in Farias & Tan (2023). Then, we refer bound massive stars in the central regions within 20% of the half-mass radius of their star cluster as _central stars_ . Similarly, massive stars beyond 20% of the half-mass radius which are in the outer regions of the star cluster are referred as _offset stars_ . Finally, massive stars that are unbound from the star cluster are referred to as _ejected stars_ . 

After dividing massive stars into subsets, we study the properties of bound and unbound companions around them. For this purpose, we have developed routines to identify bound companions around any given massive star. The routine works as follows: First, we identify the closest bound companion (a binary partner) to the massive star. Then, we replace the two stars with a center of mass particle. Next, we search for the next closest star that is bounded to this center of mass particle, hence forming a triple. If present, we replace the triple with its corresponding center of mass particle. Then, we search for the next closest bound companion. We perform this process iteratively to identify all the stars that are bound to the massive star. We start this search around the most massive star, identify its bound companions and tag them. Then, we move to the next most massive untagged star and search for its bound companions, ensuring there is no doublecounting of stars during this iterative process. This allows us to identify all the bound stars that are centered on independent primary massive stars within our star cluster.

## **2.1 Star Cluster Formation Simulations** 

In this work, we use the Turbulent Clump Core Accretion (TCCA) star cluster formation models developed by Farias et al. (2017, 2019); Farias & Tan (2023), where star clusters are formed inside magnetized, turbulent, gravitationally bound, and initially starless clumps within giant molecular clouds (GMCs). These consist of a suite of unique _𝑁_ -body simulations focused on accurately following stellar dynamics in the early stages of star cluster formation, i.e., where there is still ongoing formation of stars. These models assume individual stars and primordial binary stars form via stochastic core accretion with initial clump properties based on the Turbulent Core Accretion (TCA) model (McKee & Tan 2003). Farias et al. (2017) (hereafter, Paper I) presented the extreme case of instantaneous star cluster formation, where all stars are formed together at once and remaining gas is assumed to leave the system instantaneously according to a given global star formation efficiency (SFE, _𝜖_ ). Farias et al. (2019) and Farias & Tan (2023) (hereafter, Papers II and III, respectively) presented the case of gradual star cluster formation. In these simulations, we assume that a fraction ( _𝜖_ ) of the gas is gradually converted into stars while the remaining gas is also steadily removed from the system due to stellar feedback. This is modeled as a linear decrease of the gas reservoir (Equation 9, Paper III) until it reaches zero at the end of star formation, _𝑡★_ . The timescale over which this process occurs is set by the star formation efficiency per free-fall time, _𝜖_ ff, such that higher values of _𝜖_ ff result in shorter _𝑡★_ (see Paper III for details). The case of _𝜖_ ff = ∞ corresponds to the instantaneous case where all stars are formed at once, whereas the slowest case considered assumes _𝜖_ ff = 0.01. For this paper, we post-processed clusters formed from _𝑁_ -body models outlined in Paper III.

## 3.4. _Illustrative Implication for Seed Black Hole Growth_ 

The simulations above measure the dTDE rate as a local stellar feeding process in gas-rich dense clusters. Here we use these rates to illustrate one possible implication for black hole seed growth, without assuming that our cluster model represents the full complexity of highredshift galaxy formation. Figure 7 should therefore be read as an illustrative implication of the simulated feeding rates. A systematic study of seed black hole growth within cosmological environments requires cosmological simulations and will be presented in a companion paper.

retrieved_chunks.text: As discussed in the Introduction, the observed population of high-redshift quasars requires the existence of black hole seeds with masses of _M•_ ≳ 10[5] _M⊙_ by _z ∼_ 15. However, the formation of such massive seeds remains challenging. The light-seed scenario, in which stellar-mass black holes form from Population III stars at _z ∼_ 20–30 (Haiman & Loeb 2001; Madau & Rees 2001), generally requires prolonged super-Eddington accretion to reach the observed SMBH masses, which is difficult to sustain due to radiative and mechanical feedback from the accreting black hole (e.g., Sassano et al. 2023; Shi et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2025; Kiyuna 2026). The heavy-seed scenario through direct collapse of primordial gas clouds can produce black holes with masses of _∼_ 10[4] –10[6] _M⊙_ (e.g., Oh & Haiman 2002; Bromm & Loeb 2003; Begelman et al. 2006). Related TDE-assisted growth channels, including tidal disruptions of Population III stars by IMBH seeds, have also been proposed to boost early black hole growth (Wang et al. 2025). However, these scenarios are highly sensitive to fragmentation induced by trace amounts of dust, metals, or molecular hydrogen (Omukai et al. 2008; Latif et al. 2016; Chon & Omukai 2020). Such fragmentation may favor the formation of multiple massive stars rather than a single massive seed black hole (Chon & Omukai 2020). An alternative and increasingly favored pathway is the formation of IMBHs with masses of _∼_ 10[3] – 10[4] _M⊙_ through runaway stellar collisions in dense star clusters (e.g., Portegies Zwart et al. 2004; Rantala et al. 2024; Fujii et al. 2024; Vergara et al. 2025; Mestichelli et al. 2026). ## **2 METHODS** 

In section 2.1, we describe the _𝑁_ -body models of gradual star cluster formation used for this paper. We have post-processed these simulations to study the evolution of stellar clustering around massive stars. In section 2.2, we describe the process of identifying bound systems around massive stars, which are later compared to study how the environment and formation timescale affect these bound systems. In section 2.3, we describe how we construct projected stellar density profiles around massive stars to compare different models of massive star formation with each other and with observations.

claims.text: The Rapid Growth paper reports disk-induced tidal disruption (dTDE) stellar mass supply rates of order ≃ 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}.
The Rapid Growth paper reports that the dTDE-driven stellar disruption rate is ≃ (1–3) × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1} (statement in the paper's conclusions).

Wang et al. (Rapid Growth) give mass-dependent examples: for M• = 3 × 10^{3} M⊙ and 10^{4} M⊙ the disruption rates remain at ≃ 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}, while for M• = 3 × 10^{4} M⊙ the rate is ≃ 3 × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1}.
The Rapid Growth paper states that these dTDE mass-supply rates exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate for black holes with M• < 10^{5} M⊙.

The Rapid Growth paper explicitly tested sensitivity to the inner accretion radius: comparing RdTDE = 10^{-4} pc (fiducial) with RdTDE = 5 × 10^{-5} pc produced nearly identical disruption rates, which the paper states indicates insensitivity to the specific choice of RdTDE (inner accretion radius).

The Star Cluster Formation (TCCA) study uses high-precision N-body simulations of gradual star-cluster formation with an analytic gas potential (Turbulent Clump Core Accretion), controlled by parameters including star-formation efficiency per freefall time (ε_ff), clump mass M_cl and cloud mass surface density Σ_cloud, with gas mass linearly reduced to zero at the end of star formation t_★.

The Star Cluster Formation paper provides a routine to identify bound companions around a massive star by iteratively finding the closest bound companion, replacing the pair/triple with its center-of-mass, and continuing to build higher-order bound systems (binary → triple →...).

The Star Cluster Formation work computes quantitative clustering metrics such as the mean number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ (with mass-threshold choices), reports uncertainties (16th–84th percentile spreads and standard errors), and presents these metrics at specified cluster ages (e.g., t = 3.0 Myr).
The Star Cluster Formation paper constructs projected stellar density profiles around massive stars to compare models with observations and to diagnose clustering around massive primaries.

The Rapid Growth dTDE rates of ≃ (1–3) × 10^{-3} M⊙ yr^{-1} (52a69f9f) could be tested by supplying Wang et al.'s disk-capture and migration calculations with the star-cluster paper's quantitative inner-stellar-population outputs (e.g., ⟨N_bound⟩ and companion mass-thresholded distributions) to produce a matched estimate of the disk-crossing supply rate.

Wang et al. identify two-body relaxation refilling the disk-crossing population and formation of a stellar cusp as key processes controlling sustained dTDE rates; the Star Cluster Formation methods (the bound-companion identification and central/offset/ejected classification) can be used to quantify how many stars are bound and centrally concentrated and hence available to be scattered into disk-crossing orbits.

Because the TCCA models vary environmental parameters that set cluster compactness and velocity dispersion (Σ_cloud, M_cl, ε_ff), those N-body outputs can provide stellar distributions for different cluster compactnesses that could be combined with Wang et al.'s figure-level Rout variants (Rout = R_{sg} versus Rout = 3 R_{sg}) to probe how the dTDE supply rate responds to changes in disk outer radius across different stellar environments.

The Star Cluster Formation simulations produce time-resolved cluster snapshots (e.g., analyses at t = 3.0 Myr) while Wang et al. note their dTDE runs are limited in duration (~0.3 Myr) and that growth to ≳10^{5} M⊙ would require persistence of cluster and disk conditions for >30 Myr; therefore extending or using longer-duration N-body cluster models can directly test whether the dTDE rates reported by Wang et al. can be sustained on the >30 Myr timescale they identify as required for substantial IMBH growth.
The Rapid Growth paper's figure text includes disk-outer-radius variants labeled "Rout = Rsg" and "Rout = 3Rsg".

It also accurately identifies the star-cluster paper's N-body simulations, bound-companion identification routine, projected density profiles, and time-resolved snapshots as capabilities that can test Rapid Growth assumptions, and synthesizes how to combine these methods to refine dTDE input distributions and timescale persistence.
